Abacus

CountingPlace ValueAlgorithms
Game: Explore an abacus: move counters to build numbers in any base from 2 to 16.
How to play: Click a counter to move it towards or away from the bar. Add a second abacus and tick Sync to make one count up as the other counts down.
Look for the math

For centuries an abacus was a calculator made of pebbles, grooves and rods. Its cleverness is not the counting but the place value: the same counter means different amounts on different wires.

Wires are places

The leftmost wire is the most significant one. A wire shows a digit from 0 to one less than the radix, counted by the chips pushed towards the bar. Reading the wires left to right gives a number in that base — the display uses 0 to 9 and then A to Z for digits above nine. An empty wire is a zero: the ancient devices had no written zero symbol for centuries even though an empty groove represented it perfectly.

Carrying and borrowing

When a wire would pass its highest digit, one is carried to the wire on its left; the applet does this for you. Taking away more than a wire holds borrows from the left. The original has a small quirk: a wire holding exactly one counter is treated like an empty one during a borrow, so a long borrow can give a surprising result. The logic test compares the arithmetic with a second transcription of the applet's rules over every base from 2 to 16.

Two abaci and Sync

With Sync checked, taking counters from one abacus adds the same amount to the other at the matching wire, so the two numbers change in opposite directions. When neither side carries or borrows past an edge, their combined value stays the same — the logic test checks that on hundreds of two-abacus positions. Try it with two bases at once by switching the radix and watching how the same moves write different numbers.

Set the radix to 2 and try to make 10101. Then switch to base 16 and see what the very same counters say.
